title: Sequential Circuits — Latches & Flip-Flops
summary: Feed a gate's output back into its own input and you get memory — latches and flip-flops are that trick, plus the timing contract every one of them must satisfy.

slides.subTitle: Feedback changes everything
slides.markdown:
Every circuit in the previous topic was combinational — no memory, pure function of current inputs. **Sequential circuits** add one new idea: **feedback**, an output wired back around into an input.

That single change is what makes memory possible. A circuit with feedback can hold a state that persists even after its inputs stop driving it — the entire basis for registers, RAM, and every stateful piece of a CPU. Every latch and flip-flop in this topic is, underneath, gates plus a feedback loop.

slides.subTitle: SR latch
slides.markdown:
The **SR latch** (Set-Reset) is the simplest feedback memory cell — two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates, each gate's output feeding the other's input. **Set** (S=1) forces the stored bit to 1; **Reset** (R=1) forces it to 0; S=R=0 holds whatever was last stored.

The catch: **S=1, R=1 simultaneously is a forbidden state** — both outputs get forced to the same value, breaking the complementary Q/Q' relationship the latch is supposed to maintain, and the result when both inputs release depends on tiny circuit timing differences (a race condition baked into the gates themselves).

slides.subTitle: D latch vs D flip-flop
slides.markdown:
A **D latch** takes a Data input and a clock/enable: whenever the clock is **high** (level-sensitive), the latch continuously tracks D — it's 'transparent'. When the clock goes low, it freezes whatever D last had.

A **D flip-flop** instead samples D only at the instant the clock **transitions** (a rising or falling edge) — **edge-triggered**. This matters in a real chip: a transparent latch can let a signal race through several latches within one clock phase, while an edge-triggered flip-flop samples once per cycle, giving predictable, one-change-per-cycle behavior.

slides.subTitle: A clock edge triggering a change
slides.markdown:
An edge-triggered flip-flop only 'looks at' its data input for an instant, at the clock edge:

![A clock signal with a rising edge marked, and D and Q signals showing Q updating only at that instant](assets/flipflop-clock-edge.svg)

D can change freely at any other time without affecting Q — only the value present right at the rising edge gets captured and held until the next edge. This is what makes a chip's overall behavior predictable: every flip-flop in the design updates at the same well-defined instants, not continuously.

assets.alt: A clock signal with a rising edge marked, and D and Q signals showing Q updating only at that instant

slides.subTitle: JK and T flip-flops
slides.markdown:
**JK flip-flops** extend the SR idea but fix its forbidden state: J=K=1 causes the output to **toggle** (flip its current value) instead of racing undefined — every input combination is now well-defined.

**T (toggle) flip-flops** simplify further to a single input: T=1 toggles the state, T=0 holds it. This is exactly the building block for **binary counters** — chain T flip-flops so each one toggles on the previous stage's transition, and you get a circuit that counts in binary automatically.

slides.subTitle: Setup, hold, propagation delay
slides.markdown:
Every flip-flop has a **timing contract** it must be respected: **setup time** (how long D must be stable *before* the clock edge), **hold time** (how long D must stay stable *after* the edge), and **propagation delay** (how long after the edge until Q reflects the new value).

These aren't suggestions — they're physical requirements of the internal transistors resolving to a clean 0 or 1. Violate setup or hold and the flip-flop's output can enter an undefined, unstable in-between state rather than cleanly landing on 0 or 1.

slides.subTitle: Latches vs flip-flops
slides.markdown:
| | Latches (level-sensitive) | Flip-flops (edge-triggered) |
|---|---|---|
| Samples input | Continuously while clock is a given level | Only at the clock edge |
| Behavior across a clock phase | Transparent — can let a race condition ripple through | One clean update per cycle |
| Where used | Building block inside some flip-flop designs; some low-power/latch-based design styles | The default memory element in essentially all mainstream CPU pipelines |

CPUs standardize on flip-flops because pipeline stages need a crisp, one-state-per-cycle boundary — a transparent latch's 'leakiness' during a clock phase makes multi-stage timing analysis far harder to reason about.

slides.subTitle: Metastability
slides.markdown:
Violate setup or hold time — say, an input changes right at the clock edge from an unsynchronized external signal — and a flip-flop can enter **metastability**: its output hovers at neither a clean 0 nor 1 for an unpredictable time before resolving to one or the other, essentially at random.

This is unavoidable in principle when crossing between two independently clocked domains. The standard mitigation is a **synchronizer** — typically two flip-flops in series — giving a metastable state extra cycles to resolve before the value is used elsewhere.
